semantic_correction.stem: A client recently diagnosed with diabetes says, 'I feel overwhelmed and I am not sure how this will fit into my life.' Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.A: Acknowledge that this feels overwhelming, ask what concerns affect daily life most, identify supports, and choose one or two manageable next steps together.
options.B: Explain that adjustment usually follows a predictable sequence of emotional stages, and delay diabetes education until the client reaches acceptance.
options.C: Redirect the discussion to glucose and insulin targets first, because emotional responses can be addressed after self-management skills are established.
options.D: Reassure the client that most people adapt within several weeks, provide standard written instructions, and suggest emotional support only if distress persists.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. The American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 recommend psychosocial care for all people with diabetes as part of routine medical care using a collaborative, person-centered, culturally informed approach. The ADA specifically describes creating a supportive environment for emotional disclosure, validating the person's experience, asking open-ended questions, using empathetic listening, and applying collaborative goal setting and other coping strategies. The 2026 comprehensive medical-evaluation standards likewise recommend person-centered, culturally sensitive, strength-based communication with active listening, elicitation of individual preferences and beliefs, assessment of barriers, and collaborative care planning. A follows this approach by validating the client's distress, exploring its individual meaning, identifying supports, and choosing manageable next steps collaboratively. B is incorrect because current guidance does not require a universal fixed sequence of emotional stages before education can proceed. C is incorrect because psychosocial care is part of routine diabetes care and should not be deferred until technical self-management skills are established. D is incorrect because it imposes an unsupported adjustment timetable and delays support rather than assessing the client's current needs.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Support adjustment to a new chronic illness diagnosis with validation, open-ended assessment, person-centered communication, identification of supports and barriers, and collaborative coping/self-management planning rather than imposing a fixed emotional-stage model.
semantic_correction.source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors and Well-being to Improve Health Outcomes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; Comprehensive Medical Evaluation and Assessment of Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Diabetes Care 2026; published December 8, 2025; current articles verified August 22, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: Section 5 Psychosocial Care → Recommendation 5.42 and accompanying text: psychosocial care is part of routine diabetes care; create a supportive environment for emotional disclosure; validate experiences; ask open-ended questions; use empathetic listening; use collaborative goal setting and coping strategies. Section 4 Person-Centered Collaborative Care → Recommendation 4.1 and accompanying text: use person-centered, culturally sensitive, strength-based language and active listening; elicit preferences and beliefs; assess barriers; use open-ended questions, reflective statements, and collaborative planning.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: ADA 2026 guidance directly supports individualized, collaborative psychosocial assessment and support during diabetes care using validation, open-ended questions, active listening, assessment of barriers/supports, and collaborative goal setting rather than rigid stage-based assumptions or delayed psychosocial care.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the correct-answer length cue, rebuilt all four responses to near-equal length, freshly verified current ADA person-centered psychosocial-care guidance, and eliminated the unsupported assumption that adjustment must follow a universal fixed emotional-stage sequence.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests individualized psychosocial support after a new diabetes diagnosis with one clearly best response, balanced alternatives, current authoritative guidance, and no answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It validates the emotion, uses open-ended individualized assessment, identifies supports, and collaborates on manageable next steps in line with current ADA guidance.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. A fixed universal emotional-stage sequence is not required by current diabetes psychosocial-care guidance and should not delay education or support.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Psychosocial concerns are part of routine diabetes care and should be assessed alongside self-management needs rather than deferred.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. It imposes an unsupported timeline and delays individualized psychosocial support despite the client's current distress.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A uniquely combines validation, individualized assessment, support identification, and collaborative planning; B imposes a rigid stage model, C defers psychosocial care, and D minimizes distress with an unsupported timetable.
cueing_check: All four responses are parallel communication and care-planning strategies of comparable length and specificity; the prior uniquely-long correct response was removed.
